docs.text: What is Polygon Crusher 9000? Polygon Crusher 9000 is a Blender addon for fast, high-quality mesh decimation. It crushes dense meshes down to the triangle budget your scene needs while keeping what matters: surface shading, silhouette, UV mapping, and the hard edges of CAD and hard-surface parts. Unlike Blender's built-in Decimate, the simplifier runs as a worker subprocess, so the UI stays responsive. It is modifier-aware and runs several objects at the same time. You choose the target as a percentage, a triangle count per object, or one triangle budget for the whole selection. Built for: 3D scans, sculpts, AI-generated meshes, hard-surface and CAD parts, LOD generation. Get Started · Settings Reference · Limits Features Exact targets — ask for 80% and you get 80%. Ask for 5,000 triangles and you get 5,000. The engine removes the least visible detail first. Some options can stop a crush above the target, so check the report. See Limits . Modes — Auto looks at the mesh and picks Scan , Sculpt or Hard Surface for you, switching on only the repairs it found. See Modes . Three target modes — Percent , Count (per object), or Budget (one total for the whole selection). See Target Modes . Normal Preservation — copies the original's surface normals onto the result, so smooth shading survives heavy crushing. Hard Surface Preservation — keep borders, material borders, UV seams and sharp edges in place, and still reach the count you asked for. See Hard Surface Preservation . Protect Areas — select faces in Edit Mode (or paint a vertex group) to keep detail in faces, hands or text. See Protect Areas . Clean Mesh — repair AI-generated and scanned meshes before crushing. See Clean Mesh . Import and Crush — crush an OBJ, PLY or STL file straight from disk, for scans too big for Blender's importers. The engine reads the file; only the crushed result, with its UVs, textures, materials and vertex colors, is built in Blender. See Import and Crush . Bake Maps and Auto UVs — bake normal and base color maps onto the crushed mesh, with the base color taken from the original's image textures or vertex colors. Meshes without UVs get UVs made for them. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . LODs in one click — build a whole LOD chain from the original. See LODs . Rigs, shape keys and vertex colors carry over — the crushed copy keeps skin weights, the Armature modifier, shape keys and vertex colors, so a rigged character still poses. See Rigs, Shape Keys and Vertex Colors . Revert — delete a crushed object and bring back its original. See Keep Original and Revert . Modifier-Aware — crushes the evaluated mesh; boolean, subdivision, and the rest of the modifier stack are applied automatically. The original's modifiers stay untouched. Live Progress — Blender stays responsive during long crushes. Press ESC at any time to cancel. Session Stats — per-object triangle counts and timing, directly in the panel. Requirements Blender 4.2 or later. 4.2 is the lowest version the extension accepts and has not been tested; the add-on is tested on 5.2 OS Windows (x64), Linux (x64, ARM64), macOS (Apple Silicon) Support Questions or issues? docs.text: Benchmarks: against Blender Decimate and meshoptimizer Where it stands Two comparisons have been measured in full, both with the repo's own test harnesses, plus a first look at MeshLab on two small meshes. Nothing else has been, so this page makes no claims about Simplygon, InstaLOD, ZBrush Decimation Master or any other reducer. Against Blender Decimate (2026-10-10, engine 2.3.2): 2.2–3.0× faster on meshes of 1–7.5 million triangles, about even at 100k, slower (0.6×) on a scene of 103 small parts. The same shape at the same triangle count. Decimate also reaches its target, so exact counts are not what sets the two apart. Ahead on CAD with Hard Surface on (creases stay where they are), and on everything Decimate does not do: Keep Normals, UV-aware collapses, scan repair, Import and Crush, bakes, LOD chains, rigs and shape keys carried over. Behind with Keep UVs on a part cut into many small UV islands at a very low target, because seam vertices stay on their islands. Against meshoptimizer (2026-10-13, engine 2.7.1): The same surface error, within measurement noise, on scans, sculpts and smooth CAD at keep 10% and keep 2%; slightly lower on a small CAD block. On a hard-surface model of many parts the picture is mixed. Both tools' default settings stop short of the target on it; 2.7.1 fixed that for Polygon Crusher, and meshoptimizer's attribute setting still has the lower error at keep 10%. At keep 2% they are close. meshoptimizer is about three times faster, on one core; Polygon Crusher uses all cores. On a single core the gap would be wider. Against MeshLab (early readings, two meshes, see below): about the same at keep 10%; MeshLab's plain decimation is better on the small CAD block at keep 2%, and its UV-keeping variant is much worse there. In short: a match for the best open-source simplifier on surface error, slower per core, better integrated for Blender work, and since 2.7.1 no longer the tool that falls over on multi-part hard-surface models, without being the best one on those either. The sections below show the numbers. Against Blender Decimate Measured on 2026-10-10 with Polygon Crusher 2.3.2. This section shows how the speed figure on the store page was measured, so you can judge it yourself. These numbers still apply to 2.4.x. 2.4 changed the panel, the bake, and a Keep Normals correction that only runs on CAD and hard-surface parts. 2.4.2 added two small engine checks (no stray spike vertices, better detail in protected areas) that leave scan, sculpt and CAD results unchanged. 2.5.0 changed only the bake (base color from image textures, fewer tiny UV islands on scans); the crush itself is the same. 2.6.0 added Low Distortion under Keep UVs, which costs a few percent of crush time. 2.7.1 changed how kept edges and small pieces are handled; scans, sculpts and smooth CAD parts measure the same as before, hard-surface models with many parts do not (see Against meshoptimizer below). None of these were re-timed against Decimate. Summary Speed: 2.2–3.0× faster than Blender's Decimate on meshes of 1–7.5 million triangles. About the same at 100k. Slower on many small parts. Shape: about the same as Decimate at the same triangle count. On CAD parts with Hard Surface on, creases stay exactly in place. With Keep UVs on, very low targets on parts cut into many small UV islands keep less shape, because seam vertices stay on their islands. Imported scans: meshes imported from glTF or FBX are often split into separate pieces along their UV seams. Turn on Clean Mesh for these, or open edges can shrink and leave gaps. Method Blender 5.2.2 LTS, run headless. Windows 11, Intel i7-12700H (20 threads), 64 GB RAM. Test meshes: a CC0 Poly Haven rock scan (1.26M triangles), a smaller boulder scan (98k), a 1.0M-triangle synthetic sculpt, a 7.56M-triangle subdivided scan, a CAD part (5.1k), and a set of 103 hard-surface parts (200k total). Blender: Decimate modifier in Collapse mode, ratio = target ÷ input, applied to a new mesh. Polygon Crusher: the add-on's own pipeline (read the mesh with UVs and normals, run the native engine with an exact target, build the result with UVs and custom normals). No bake. Time: end to end, median of 3 runs. Shape loss: distance from the original surface to the result, as % of the bounding-box diagonal (mean / max). Case Decimate (mean / max) PC, Keep UVs on PC, Keep UVs off Rock scan 1.26M → 20k 0.025 / 0.42 0.024 / 0.81 0.023 / 0.79 Rock scan 1.26M → 2k 0.085 / 1.07 0.092 / 1.56 0.079 / 1.38 Boulder scan 98k → 5k 0.086 / 0.79 0.084 / 1.67 0.083 / 1.61 Hard-surface part 13.8k → 3.4k 0.098 / 4.48 0.213 / 9.06 0.106 / 1.88 CAD part 5.1k → 1k, Hard Surface on 0.0026 / 0.071 0.0000 / 0.0001 0.0000 / 0.0001 The hard-surface part has many small UV islands, so with Keep UVs on its thin cables lose the most. Against meshoptimizer Measured on 2026-10-13, engine 2.7.0 and then 2.7.1, against meshoptimizer v1.3 (the open-source simplifier behind Godot and the glTF tools), built from source. One Windows machine. This is the test that found the two 2.7.1 fixes, so it is shown here with both results. Method The engine binary alone, not the add-on, on OBJ files: the 1.26M rock scan and the 98k boulder scan from above, a 60k noisy scan, the 1.0M sculpt, a 5k sculpt, the 5.1k CAD block, an 83k smooth CAD part, and an electricity pole of 103 parts (13.4k triangles). Targets: keep 10% and keep 2% of the triangles. Polygon Crusher runs with the flags its mode would use (Hard Surface for the CAD parts and the pole, Scan and Sculpt for the rest). meshoptimizer runs with its defaults and, where it does better, with its attribute settings (normals and UVs, permissive). Scans, sculpts and smooth CAD: the same error At keep 10%, mean error of the two tools, Polygon Crusher / meshoptimizer: Case Mean error (PC / mo) Worst (PC / mo) Rock scan 1.26M → 126k 0.069 / 0.069 0.16 / 0.16 Boulder scan 98k → 9.8k 0.123 / 0.127 0.28 / 0.28 Noisy scan 60k → 6k 0.173 / 0.182 0.58 / 0.48 Sculpt 1.0M → 101k 0.101 / 0.101 0.24 / 0.24 Smooth CAD part 83k → 8.3k 0.163 / 0.163 0.40 / 0.39 CAD block 5.1k → 512 0.163 / 0.188 0.38 / 0.52 Keep 2% looks the same: the two tools are within measurement noise of each other on every one of these, before and after 2.7.1. (The 1.26M scan and the 1.0M sculpt were only run with the 2.7.0 engine; 2.7.1 did not change the scan or sculpt path.) The multi-part pole: what 2.7.1 fixed The pole has borders, material edges, seams and sharp edges everywhere, and 103 separate pieces. It is where the old engine failed. Pole 13.4k, keep 2% Triangles Mean error Worst error PC 2.7.0, plain crush 268 2.48 20.7 PC 2.7.0, Hard Surface mode 7,081 (stalled at 53%) 0.21 3.3 PC 2.7.1, plain crush 266 0.75 5.2 PC 2.7.1, Hard Surface mode 266 0.42 4.2 meshoptimizer, defaults 2,788 (stopped at 21%) 0.27 5.9 meshoptimizer, attributes 260 0.39 5.7 At keep 2% the 2.7.0 plain crush disintegrated: whole beams went while small insulators stayed, hence a worst-case error of 20.7% of the model's size. In 2.7.1 every piece keeps a minimum until the budget is spent, and the worst case is 5.2%. Hard Surface mode on 2.7.0 stalled at about half the triangles at both targets (7,091 at keep 10%, 7,081 at keep 2%), because the kept edges were a hard lock. In 2.7.1 it reaches 1,337 and 266. meshoptimizer with its defaults also stops short on this model, at 2,816 triangles whatever you ask; with its attribute settings it reaches the count. At keep 10% that setting has the lowest error of all the runs (mean 0.17, worst 0.84, against 0.23 and 1.30 for Hard Surface mode). At keep 2% the two are close: lower mean for meshoptimizer, lower worst case for Polygon Crusher. On the 5.1k CAD block, Hard Surface mode at keep 10% halved its error (mean 0.31 → 0.16, worst 1.23 → 0.38) because the hole rims are no longer locked. At keep 2% it now reaches 102 triangles where 2.7.0 stopped at 272, and that costs shape: mean error 1.98 against 1.13 at the old, higher count. Reaching a very low count on a small part is a trade you choose by picking the target. Speed meshoptimizer is about three times faster: 0.8 s against 2.3 s on the 1.26M scan at keep 10%, 0.5 s against 1.3 s on the 1.0M sculpt. It gets there on one core; Polygon Crusher spreads its work over all of them. Both are well under the time Blender needs to build the result mesh. Limits of this test Engine against library, both run from Python on one Windows machine. The add-on's own read, build and bake steps are not included, and neither is any glTF or game-engine pipeline around meshoptimizer. meshoptimizer has more settings than the two tried here; a tuned run may do better on the pole. Error is a surface-distance measurement. It does not see shading, UV stretch or whether a hole is still round; look at the result. Against MeshLab: early readings MeshLab's Quadric Edge Collapse Decimation (through pymeshlab 2025.7) is the reducer most people run on scans outside game studios. It was added to the bake-off harness on 2026-10-13 and has so far been run on two of the eight fixtures, on Linux, with the 2.7.1 engine. Two small meshes are not a verdict; the full set, on the Windows machine used above, is still to come. Same error measure as the meshoptimizer section; Polygon Crusher with its mode's flags, MeshLab with the filter's defaults ("plain") and with the with-texture variant that keeps the UV layout ("UVs"). Case Polygon Crusher (mean / worst) MeshLab plain MeshLab UVs CAD block 5.1k → 512 0.163 / 0.38 0.169 / 0.41 0.50 / 4.0 CAD block 5.1k → 102 1.98 / 12.1 0.99 / 5.4 3.5 / 21.8 Sculpt 5.1k → 514 0.114 / 0.23 0.120 / 0.27 0.130 / 0.27 Sculpt 5.1k → 102 0.364 / 0.85 0.437 / 1.87 0.59 / 2.3 At keep 10% the two are within a few percent of each other on both meshes. At keep 2% on the CAD block MeshLab's plain decimation is clearly better: half the mean error, half the worst case. Polygon Crusher's Hard Surface mode is paying there for reaching 102 triangles while still favouring the kept edges; the plain crush (no edges kept) scores 1.63 / 10.2, also behind MeshLab. This is the one case so far where another tool is ahead on a plain surface-error measure, and it will be checked on the full set. Part of the gap is the 2.7.1 decision to always reach the count: the 2.7.0 engine stopped at 272 triangles on this block with a lower error than 2.7.1 gets at 102. Keep 2% of a 5,000-triangle part is 102 triangles, which is below where either tool keeps the shape; on a part this small, pick the target by looking at the result, not the percentage. MeshLab's UV-keeping variant is far worse on the CAD block at both targets: the seams constrain it the way Keep UVs constrains any simplifier, and this block has many of them. On the sculpt Polygon Crusher is ahead at both targets, more so at keep 2%. Times are not comparable yet: a different machine from the rest of this page, and meshes this small finish in a few hundredths of a second either way.

docs.text: MeshLab's Quadric Edge Collapse Decimation (through pymeshlab 2025.7) is the reducer most people run on scans outside game studios. It was added to the bake-off harness on 2026-10-13 and has so far been run on two of the eight fixtures, on Linux, with the 2.7.1 engine. Two small meshes are not a verdict; the full set, on the Windows machine used above, is still to come. Same error measure as the meshoptimizer section; Polygon Crusher with its mode's flags, MeshLab with the filter's defaults ("plain") and with the with-texture variant that keeps the UV layout ("UVs"). Case Polygon Crusher (mean / worst) MeshLab plain MeshLab UVs CAD block 5.1k → 512 0.163 / 0.38 0.169 / 0.41 0.50 / 4.0 CAD block 5.1k → 102 1.98 / 12.1 0.99 / 5.4 3.5 / 21.8 Sculpt 5.1k → 514 0.114 / 0.23 0.120 / 0.27 0.130 / 0.27 Sculpt 5.1k → 102 0.364 / 0.85 0.437 / 1.87 0.59 / 2.3 At keep 10% the two are within a few percent of each other on both meshes. At keep 2% on the CAD block MeshLab's plain decimation is clearly better: half the mean error, half the worst case. Polygon Crusher's Hard Surface mode is paying there for reaching 102 triangles while still favouring the kept edges; the plain crush (no edges kept) scores 1.63 / 10.2, also behind MeshLab. This is the one case so far where another tool is ahead on a plain surface-error measure, and it will be checked on the full set. Part of the gap is the 2.7.1 decision to always reach the count: the 2.7.0 engine stopped at 272 triangles on this block with a lower error than 2.7.1 gets at 102. Keep 2% of a 5,000-triangle part is 102 triangles, which is below where either tool keeps the shape; on a part this small, pick the target by looking at the result, not the percentage. MeshLab's UV-keeping variant is far worse on the CAD block at both targets: the seams constrain it the way Keep UVs constrains any simplifier, and this block has many of them. On the sculpt Polygon Crusher is ahead at both targets, more so at keep 2%. Times are not comparable yet: a different machine from the rest of this page, and meshes this small finish in a few hundredths of a second either way.

docs.text: Limits Polygon Crusher 9000 does not always reach the target. This page lists what can stop it, and what the report tells you. After every crush, Blender's status bar shows a report: triangles before and after, time taken, and any warnings. Always check the "after" count. The result can stop above the target The crush aims for your target, but some things stop it early: Protect Area. Strong protection on large areas can leave the result above the target. Broken geometry. Duplicate or zero-area faces block collapses. Clean Mesh runs by itself on meshes with many duplicate vertices or zero-area triangles. Otherwise, with no preserve options on, the report says the mesh may be broken and suggests Clean Mesh . If Clean Mesh is already on, it says the mesh cannot be reduced further without breaking its shape. The report only raises this warning when the result is clearly above the target (more than 20% over), so small differences do not show up as warnings. Up to 2.7.0 the Preserve options (Borders, Materials, UV Seams, Sharp Edges) could stop a crush too, because a kept edge was a hard lock. Since 2.7.1 a kept edge is a cost instead, and the crush reaches the count you asked for. What a very low target costs on such a model is shape, not triangles: see What a very low target costs . Small pieces at heavy reductions A model made of many separate pieces (a pole with its insulators, a set of screws) loses whole pieces when the target is a small fraction of its triangles. Since 2.7.1 every connected piece keeps a minimum number of triangles until the error budget is truly spent, and then pieces go in order of how little they matter, smallest first. At an extreme target pieces still disappear; raise the target, or put a Protect Area on the ones that must stay. Remove Small Pieces under Clean Mesh is a different thing: it deletes loose bits before the crush, on purpose. Objects can be skipped An object is left untouched, and named in the report, when it: has no geometry after modifiers, has fewer than 4 triangles, or gets no triangles in a Budget crush. If every selected object is already at or below the target, the copies are left unchanged and the report says so. Scans and noisy meshes: Sharp Edges On a scan-like mesh, almost every edge has a small bend because of surface noise. Treating all of them as sharp would lock the whole mesh. So on meshes that read as scans (mostly noise, few flat faces), angle-based Sharp detection is skipped . Only the edges you marked Sharp in Blender are kept. The report names the objects where this happened. If you want specific edges kept on a scan, mark them Sharp yourself first. Very low targets on dense CAD Very low targets on dense CAD meshes, a few hundred triangles, can fold the walls of holes together. This leaves edges that are shared by three or more faces (non-manifold edges). The report warns when a crushed copy has more of these edges than its source. If that matters for your export or for baking, raise the target. Baking Base Color is baked from the image textures feeding each material's Base Color, or from vertex colors when a material has none. Colors made by procedural nodes (Noise, Gradient, a plain color value) are not baked. An object with neither textures nor vertex colors is skipped for Base Color, and the report says so. A bake needs UVs on the crushed mesh. Meshes without UVs are unwrapped automatically. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . The baked maps are connected in copies of the materials. If an input was already connected there, the old link is replaced. The bake happens after the crush. A failed bake is listed in the report as a note and the crushed mesh is kept. Rigs, shape keys and vertex colors Skin weights, the Armature modifier, shape keys and vertex colors carry over to the crushed copy, with a few limits: shape keys are dropped when a modifier changes the vertex count, and vertex colors are skipped on sources over 3 million triangles. See Rigs, Shape Keys and Vertex Colors . Keep UVs Keep UVs is off by default (the Scan, Sculpt and Hard Surface modes turn it on when the mesh has UVs). Turn it on only when the crushed mesh must keep its UV layout. UV transfer quality depends on how much the topology changed. Moderate reductions give the cleanest results. Very heavy reductions can stretch UVs near seams. Turn on UV Seams to hold the seam lines in place. Low Distortion refuses collapses that would fold or flatten a face's texture mapping. Up to 2.7.0 that could leave the result about 12% above the target on a mesh with many seams. Since 2.7.1 the crush relaxes the UV rules in stages once it runs out of safe collapses, so the target is reached; the last few percent of a very low target can then show some stretch near seams. Revert Revert needs the original. It only works when the crush was made with Keep Original on, or with Make LODs. See Keep Original and Revert . Import and Crush Reads .obj , .ply (ascii and binary) and .stl (ascii and binary). Other formats (glTF, FBX, USD) have to go through Blender's own importer. Normals in the file are ignored; the result is shaded smooth. Keep Normals, Protect Area, Bake and LODs do not apply to an imported file. A texture is only connected when the image is next to the model and Keep UVs is on. Textures other than the base color ( map_Kd ) are not read. Faces with more than four corners are split as fans. A concave n-gon can come out wrong; scans do not have those. Memory: the engine needs about 1 GB of RAM per 3 million triangles in the file. A 32 million triangle OBJ (2.5 GB on disk) peaked at 10 GB and crushed to 200,000 triangles in 72 seconds. On a 16 GB machine, stay under about 40 million triangles. Platform Blender 4.2 or later. 4.2 is the lowest version the extension accepts and has not been tested; the add-on is tested on Blender 5.2. Windows x64, Linux x64, Linux ARM64 and macOS Apple Silicon have bundled native binaries. Intel Macs have no bundled binary. The add-on needs its native binary. There is no Python fallback. If the binary is missing, the panel shows "Native binary not found" and Crush does not run.

docs.text: Settings Reference All settings are in the Polygon Crusher 9000 panel. Open the 3D Viewport sidebar (press N ) and click the 9000 Toolkit tab. The panel starts collapsed every time you open Blender or load a file. The panel has two levels: The main panel shows a status line, the Mode menu, the Target box, and the Crush and Revert buttons. For most models this is all you need. Advanced is a collapsed section under it. It holds Preserve , Protect Area , Bake , Clean Mesh , LODs and Output (Keep Original and the Last Crush results) as groups that fold on their own, each with a line saying what it is for. A mode opens the groups it uses and folds the rest; nothing is hidden. Options that do not apply right now are greyed out instead of hidden. For example, Strength is grey until a Protect Area is set. Status line The first line of the panel says what it is looking at: the number of selected meshes and their triangle total. With nothing selected it says "Select a mesh object to start". Mode Dropdown — default Auto What kind of model this is. A mode sets the Preserve and Clean Mesh values for you; see Modes . Auto looks at the selected mesh and shows what it found under the menu ("Looks like a scan: rough surface all over. Found: 120 spikes, 11 small holes"), then applies Scan, Sculpt or Hard Surface. Meshes over 600,000 triangles show a Detect button instead of looking by themselves. Scan , Sculpt , Hard Surface apply that mode's values. Custom is your own settings. Changing a mode-controlled value by hand shows Custom (from Scan) and a Reset to Scan defaults button. What's on When anything inside Advanced is switched on, a line under Crush lists it, for example "On: Keep UVs · Clean mesh · Spikes · Holes". So a folded group never hides what the next crush will do. When Keep Original is off, a warning under Crush says the original will be deleted. Target The Target section decides how many triangles you end up with. See Target Modes for how to choose between the three modes. Target Mode Three buttons: Percent , Count , Budget — default Percent Percent — remove a share of the triangles. Count — crush each selected object to a triangle count. Budget — one triangle total for the whole selection. The control below the buttons changes with the mode. Preset (Percent mode only) Dropdown with + and − buttons — default Custom Presets save and recall a set of settings. See Presets below. Reduction (Percent mode) Slider — 1% to 99% — default 50% Percentage of triangles to remove. 50% removes half of them. Dragging the slider covers 5% to 95%. You can type a value from 1% to 99%. The result never has fewer than 4 triangles. Target Triangles (Count mode) Number — minimum 4 — default 5000 The triangle count each selected object is crushed to. If an object already has fewer triangles than this, it is not made bigger: the target is clamped to the object's own triangle count. Total Triangles (Budget mode) Number — minimum 4 — default 100,000 The triangle total for all selected objects together. Triangle readout Under the target control, the panel shows before → after triangles , added up over the selected meshes. It uses the same rounding as the crush. The readout is hidden while Make LODs is on. The "after" number is the target, not a promise. See Limits . Import and Crush... Button under Crush Opens a file browser for an .obj , .ply or .stl file. The engine reads the file and crushes it; only the result is built in Blender. The file browser's side panel shows the Target, the Mode menu, Keep UVs (and textures) with Low Distortion , Clean Mesh with the three Scan Repair switches, and an OBJ is Y up switch. See Import and Crush . Advanced Everything below lives in the Advanced section. It starts collapsed; click its header to open it. Inside, each group ( Preserve , Protect Area , Bake , Clean Mesh , LODs , Output ) has its own fold arrow and a line under its title saying what it is for. Preserve Keep Normals Toggle button — default on Copies the original's surface normals onto the crushed mesh, so smooth shading survives even when the topology changes a lot. Crease corners keep their own normals. Leave this on in almost all cases. Turning it off gives flat, faceted shading on smooth surfaces. Greyed out while Normal Map baking is on. The bake uses the crushed mesh's own smooth shading instead. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Keep UVs Toggle button — default off Carries the active UV map through the crush, so textures still line up. If the mesh has no UVs, this does nothing. Turn it on when the crushed mesh must keep its UV layout. With it off, baking makes new UVs for the crushed copy. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Low Distortion Checkbox under Keep UVs, default on , greyed out unless Keep UVs is on. A collapse that would fold a face's texture mapping over itself, or flatten it to a line, is refused and the crush picks another edge. This is what leaves smeared or mirrored texture patches on a heavily crushed scan. Costs a few percent of crush time. Since 2.7.1 the crush still reaches the target with it on (it relaxes the rule in stages once it runs out of safe collapses). Turn it off for the plain crush (the 2.5.x behaviour). Keep in place The four options below keep edges where they are. Since 2.7.1 a kept edge is a cost rather than a lock: the crush touches it last and still reaches the count you asked for. Hard Surface mode turns them all on and sets Sharp Angle to 30° . See Hard Surface Preservation . Borders Toggle button — default off Keeps open borders (holes and cut edges) in place. Materials Toggle button — default off Keeps the borders between materials in place. UV Seams Toggle button — default off Keeps UV seams in place, so textures do not smear across them. Needs Keep UVs . The button is greyed out when Keep UVs is off. Sharp Edges Toggle button — default off Keeps hard edges crisp: edges you marked Sharp, plus edges sharper than Sharp Angle . Bumps from scan noise are ignored. On a mesh that looks like a scan, only the edges you marked Sharp are kept. The crushed mesh gets these edges marked Sharp too. Sharp Angle Angle — 1° to 180° — default 30° Edges where two faces meet at more than this angle count as sharp. Greyed out unless Sharp Edges is on. Protect Area Its own group in Advanced. Add and Remove buttons, and a vertex group field — default empty Marks areas that keep more detail. In Edit Mode, select faces, edges or vertices and click Add . They go into a vertex group named Protected (or the group already in the field), and the field fills in. Remove takes the selected parts back out. Both buttons only work in Edit Mode. You can also pick a vertex group you painted yourself in the field. When the active object is a mesh, the field lists that object's vertex groups. See Protect Areas . Strength Slider — 0% to 100% — default 50% How strongly the Protect Area resists crushing. Greyed out until a Protect Area is set. Blur Slider — 0% to 100% — default 5% How far the protection fades out from the marked area, as a share of the object's size. 0% makes a hard edge. Dragging covers 0% to 25%; you can type up to 100%. Greyed out until a Protect Area is set. Show Heatmap Toggle button — default off Colors the selected objects in the viewport by how strongly each part is protected, with the Blur fade included: blue is free to crush, red is fully protected. It is only a viewport overlay; nothing is added to the scene. Bake Bakes the original's detail onto the crushed mesh as texture maps. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Normal Map Toggle button — default off Bakes the original's surface detail into a normal map and connects it in copies of the crushed mesh's materials. Base Color Toggle button — default off Bakes the original's color into a base color map and connects it in copies of the crushed mesh's materials: the image textures feeding Base Color in its materials, or its vertex colors (active color attribute) where a material has no image. Objects with neither are skipped. Size Dropdown — 512 , 1K , 2K , 4K — default 2K Resolution of the baked maps. Greyed out until Normal Map or Base Color is on. Normal Y Dropdown — OpenGL or DirectX — default OpenGL Green channel convention of the saved normal map. OpenGL (green up): Blender, Unity, Godot. DirectX (green down): Unreal. It still looks correct in Blender. Greyed out unless Normal Map is on. Save To Dropdown — Blend File Folder or Custom Folder — default Blend File Folder Where the baked maps are saved. Blend File Folder — the same folder as the .blend file. If the file has never been saved, the maps are packed into the .blend instead. The panel shows "Unsaved: maps get packed". Custom Folder — a folder you pick in the Folder field. Paths that start with // are relative to the .blend file. If the field is empty, Crush stops and asks you to pick a folder. Clean Mesh Clean Mesh Checkbox — default off Repairs the mesh before crushing. See Clean Mesh . Remove Small Pieces Slider (labelled Small Pieces in the panel) — 0% to 5% — default 0.1% Deletes loose pieces that are smaller than this share of the mesh's triangles. 0% keeps every piece. Greyed out unless Clean Mesh is on. Scan Repair Three switches under Clean Mesh, greyed out unless it is on. Scan mode and Auto tick them from what the engine finds. See Scan Repair . Cut Floor (checkbox, default off) with Height (0% to 50%, default 0% = find the floor by itself): removes the table or ground captured under the model. Remove Spikes (checkbox, default off): pulls points shot out of the surface back in and drops long stretched faces. Fill Holes (checkbox, default off) with Size (0.1% to 50%, default 5% ): closes holes whose outline is up to this share of the model's size. LODs Make LODs Checkbox — default off Makes a chain of LODs instead of one crushed copy. While it is on, the Target section and Keep Original are greyed out, and the Crush button reads Crush LODs . See LODs . Levels Number — 1 to 8 — default 3 How many LOD levels to make. The original stays as LOD0. Ratio Slider — 5% to 95% — default 50% The share of triangles each level keeps compared to the level before it. With 50% , the levels have 50%, 25%, 12.5% of the original, and so on. When an object is active, the panel lists the triangle count of every level under these two controls. Levels and Ratio are greyed out until Make LODs is on. Output The last group in Advanced: where the result goes, and the last crush. Keep Original Checkbox — default on When on, the original object is hidden (eye icon off) after the crush, so you can compare or go back. When off, the original is deleted and only the crushed result remains. Greyed out while Make LODs is on, because LODs always keep the original. Revert only works when the original was kept. See Keep Original and Revert . Crush and Revert These sit in the main panel, under the Target box. Crush — the main button for every mode. It is available when at least one mesh object is selected. While a crush runs, the button turns into a progress bar. Press ESC to cancel. Revert — the small icon button next to Crush. Deletes the selected crushed object and brings back its original. Greyed out when there is nothing to revert. See Keep Original and Revert . When the native binary is missing, the panel shows "Native binary not found" and Crush refuses to run. See Troubleshooting . Presets Presets work in Percent mode only. The preset row has a dropdown and + and − buttons. Built-in presets set the amount only: Light · 25% , Medium · 50% , Heavy · 75% , Extreme · 90% . What to keep is the Mode 's job, so picking one leaves Keep UVs and the Preserve options alone (before 2.7.0 they switched Keep UVs off). A .blend saved with one of the older built-in presets (from before 2.4.0) opens with the dropdown on Custom . Its values are kept. A preset you save stores: Reduction, Keep Normals, Keep UVs, the four Preserve options, and Sharp Angle, and applies all of them (the Mode then shows Custom ). It does not store the target count, Protect, Bake, Clean Mesh, or LOD settings. + — save the current values as a new preset. You type a name. Saving under the name of one of your own presets replaces it. You cannot use a built-in preset name. − — delete the selected preset. It is only enabled for presets you saved, and it asks you to confirm. Built-in presets cannot be deleted. Your presets are kept in the add-on preferences, so they stay after you restart Blender. Custom means no preset is selected. If you change Reduction, Keep Normals, Keep UVs, a Preserve option or Sharp Angle by hand, the dropdown goes back to Custom . Last Crush Under Keep Original in the Output group. It shows the most recent crush of the active crushed object: Object — the crushed object's name. Triangles — before → after. Total time — the whole crush for this object. Passes — how many passes the engine made. Click Details to see the time of each phase: Phase What it measures Extract Reading the source mesh Write Writing the input for the native binary Crush The native simplifier Read Reading the binary's output Build Creating the new Blender mesh and object Bake Normals Transferring the original's normals (Keep Normals) "Bake Normals" here is the Keep Normals transfer. It is not the normal map bake. When several objects are selected, their crushes run at the same time, so the phase timings can add up to more than the wall-clock time. That is expected. The numbers are only kept for the current Blender session. If you select an object that was not crushed in this session, it says there are no stats for it.

docs.text: The first line of the panel says what it is looking at: the number of selected meshes and their triangle total. With nothing selected it says "Select a mesh object to start".

Auto looks at the selected mesh and shows what it found under the menu ("Looks like a scan: rough surface all over. Found: 120 spikes, 11 small holes"), then applies Scan, Sculpt or Hard Surface. Meshes over 600,000 triangles show a Detect button instead of looking by themselves. Scan , Sculpt , Hard Surface apply that mode's values. Custom is your own settings. Changing a mode-controlled value by hand shows Custom (from Scan) and a Reset to Scan defaults button.
docs.title: Mode

docs.text: When anything inside Advanced is switched on, a line under Crush lists it, for example "On: Keep UVs · Clean mesh · Spikes · Holes". So a folded group never hides what the next crush will do. When Keep Original is off, a warning under Crush says the original will be deleted.

docs.text: The Target section decides how many triangles you end up with. See Target Modes for how to choose between the three modes.
docs.title: Target

docs.text: Three buttons: Percent , Count , Budget — default Percent Percent — remove a share of the triangles. Count — crush each selected object to a triangle count. Budget — one triangle total for the whole selection. The control below the buttons changes with the mode.
docs.title: Target Mode

docs.text: Dropdown with + and − buttons — default Custom Presets save and recall a set of settings. See Presets below.
docs.title: Preset (Percent mode only)

docs.text: Slider — 1% to 99% — default 50% Percentage of triangles to remove. 50% removes half of them. Dragging the slider covers 5% to 95%. You can type a value from 1% to 99%. The result never has fewer than 4 triangles.
docs.title: Reduction (Percent mode)

docs.text: Number — minimum 4 — default 5000 The triangle count each selected object is crushed to. If an object already has fewer triangles than this, it is not made bigger: the target is clamped to the object's own triangle count.
docs.title: Target Triangles (Count mode)

docs.text: Number — minimum 4 — default 100,000 The triangle total for all selected objects together.
docs.title: Total Triangles (Budget mode)

docs.text: Under the target control, the panel shows before → after triangles , added up over the selected meshes. It uses the same rounding as the crush. The readout is hidden while Make LODs is on. The "after" number is the target, not a promise. See Limits .
docs.title: Triangle readout

docs.text: Button under Crush Opens a file browser for an .obj , .ply or .stl file. The engine reads the file and crushes it; only the result is built in Blender. The file browser's side panel shows the Target, the Mode menu, Keep UVs (and textures) with Low Distortion , Clean Mesh with the three Scan Repair switches, and an OBJ is Y up switch. See Import and Crush .
docs.title: Import and Crush...

docs.text: Everything below lives in the Advanced section. It starts collapsed; click its header to open it. Inside, each group ( Preserve , Protect Area , Bake , Clean Mesh , LODs , Output ) has its own fold arrow and a line under its title saying what it is for.
docs.title: Advanced

docs.text: Toggle button — default on Copies the original's surface normals onto the crushed mesh, so smooth shading survives even when the topology changes a lot. Crease corners keep their own normals. Leave this on in almost all cases. Turning it off gives flat, faceted shading on smooth surfaces. Greyed out while Normal Map baking is on. The bake uses the crushed mesh's own smooth shading instead. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs .
docs.title: Keep Normals

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Carries the active UV map through the crush, so textures still line up. If the mesh has no UVs, this does nothing. Turn it on when the crushed mesh must keep its UV layout. With it off, baking makes new UVs for the crushed copy. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs .
docs.title: Keep UVs

docs.text: Checkbox under Keep UVs, default on , greyed out unless Keep UVs is on. A collapse that would fold a face's texture mapping over itself, or flatten it to a line, is refused and the crush picks another edge. This is what leaves smeared or mirrored texture patches on a heavily crushed scan. Costs a few percent of crush time. Since 2.7.1 the crush still reaches the target with it on (it relaxes the rule in stages once it runs out of safe collapses). Turn it off for the plain crush (the 2.5.x behaviour).
docs.title: Low Distortion

docs.text: The four options below keep edges where they are. Since 2.7.1 a kept edge is a cost rather than a lock: the crush touches it last and still reaches the count you asked for. Hard Surface mode turns them all on and sets Sharp Angle to 30° . See Hard Surface Preservation .
docs.title: Keep in place

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Keeps open borders (holes and cut edges) in place.
docs.title: Borders

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Keeps the borders between materials in place.
docs.title: Materials

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Keeps UV seams in place, so textures do not smear across them. Needs Keep UVs . The button is greyed out when Keep UVs is off.
docs.title: UV Seams

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Keeps hard edges crisp: edges you marked Sharp, plus edges sharper than Sharp Angle . Bumps from scan noise are ignored. On a mesh that looks like a scan, only the edges you marked Sharp are kept. The crushed mesh gets these edges marked Sharp too.
docs.title: Sharp Edges

docs.text: Angle — 1° to 180° — default 30° Edges where two faces meet at more than this angle count as sharp. Greyed out unless Sharp Edges is on.
docs.title: Sharp Angle

docs.text: Its own group in Advanced. Add and Remove buttons, and a vertex group field — default empty Marks areas that keep more detail. In Edit Mode, select faces, edges or vertices and click Add . They go into a vertex group named Protected (or the group already in the field), and the field fills in. Remove takes the selected parts back out. Both buttons only work in Edit Mode. You can also pick a vertex group you painted yourself in the field. When the active object is a mesh, the field lists that object's vertex groups. See Protect Areas .
docs.title: Protect Area

docs.text: Slider — 0% to 100% — default 50% How strongly the Protect Area resists crushing. Greyed out until a Protect Area is set.
docs.title: Strength

docs.text: Slider — 0% to 100% — default 5% How far the protection fades out from the marked area, as a share of the object's size. 0% makes a hard edge. Dragging covers 0% to 25%; you can type up to 100%. Greyed out until a Protect Area is set.
docs.title: Blur

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Colors the selected objects in the viewport by how strongly each part is protected, with the Blur fade included: blue is free to crush, red is fully protected. It is only a viewport overlay; nothing is added to the scene.
docs.title: Show Heatmap

docs.text: Bakes the original's detail onto the crushed mesh as texture maps. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs .
docs.title: Bake

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Bakes the original's surface detail into a normal map and connects it in copies of the crushed mesh's materials.
docs.title: Normal Map

docs.text: Toggle button — default off Bakes the original's color into a base color map and connects it in copies of the crushed mesh's materials: the image textures feeding Base Color in its materials, or its vertex colors (active color attribute) where a material has no image. Objects with neither are skipped.
docs.title: Base Color

docs.text: Dropdown — 512 , 1K , 2K , 4K — default 2K Resolution of the baked maps. Greyed out until Normal Map or Base Color is on.
docs.title: Size

docs.text: Dropdown — OpenGL or DirectX — default OpenGL Green channel convention of the saved normal map. OpenGL (green up): Blender, Unity, Godot. DirectX (green down): Unreal. It still looks correct in Blender. Greyed out unless Normal Map is on.
docs.title: Normal Y

docs.text: Dropdown — Blend File Folder or Custom Folder — default Blend File Folder Where the baked maps are saved. Blend File Folder — the same folder as the .blend file. If the file has never been saved, the maps are packed into the .blend instead. The panel shows "Unsaved: maps get packed". Custom Folder — a folder you pick in the Folder field. Paths that start with // are relative to the .blend file. If the field is empty, Crush stops and asks you to pick a folder.
docs.title: Save To

docs.text: Checkbox — default off Repairs the mesh before crushing. See Clean Mesh .
docs.title: Clean Mesh

docs.text: Slider (labelled Small Pieces in the panel) — 0% to 5% — default 0.1% Deletes loose pieces that are smaller than this share of the mesh's triangles. 0% keeps every piece. Greyed out unless Clean Mesh is on.
docs.title: Remove Small Pieces

docs.text: Three switches under Clean Mesh, greyed out unless it is on. Scan mode and Auto tick them from what the engine finds. See Scan Repair . Cut Floor (checkbox, default off) with Height (0% to 50%, default 0% = find the floor by itself): removes the table or ground captured under the model. Remove Spikes (checkbox, default off): pulls points shot out of the surface back in and drops long stretched faces. Fill Holes (checkbox, default off) with Size (0.1% to 50%, default 5% ): closes holes whose outline is up to this share of the model's size.
docs.title: Scan Repair

docs.text: Checkbox — default off Makes a chain of LODs instead of one crushed copy. While it is on, the Target section and Keep Original are greyed out, and the Crush button reads Crush LODs . See LODs .
docs.title: Make LODs

docs.text: Number — 1 to 8 — default 3 How many LOD levels to make. The original stays as LOD0.
docs.title: Levels

docs.text: Slider — 5% to 95% — default 50% The share of triangles each level keeps compared to the level before it. With 50% , the levels have 50%, 25%, 12.5% of the original, and so on. When an object is active, the panel lists the triangle count of every level under these two controls. Levels and Ratio are greyed out until Make LODs is on.
docs.title: Ratio

docs.text: The last group in Advanced: where the result goes, and the last crush.
docs.title: Output

docs.text: Checkbox — default on When on, the original object is hidden (eye icon off) after the crush, so you can compare or go back. When off, the original is deleted and only the crushed result remains. Greyed out while Make LODs is on, because LODs always keep the original. Revert only works when the original was kept. See Keep Original and Revert .
docs.title: Keep Original

docs.text: These sit in the main panel, under the Target box. Crush — the main button for every mode. It is available when at least one mesh object is selected. While a crush runs, the button turns into a progress bar. Press ESC to cancel. Revert — the small icon button next to Crush. Deletes the selected crushed object and brings back its original. Greyed out when there is nothing to revert. See Keep Original and Revert . When the native binary is missing, the panel shows "Native binary not found" and Crush refuses to run. See Troubleshooting .
docs.title: Crush and Revert

docs.text: Presets work in Percent mode only. The preset row has a dropdown and + and − buttons. Built-in presets set the amount only: Light · 25% , Medium · 50% , Heavy · 75% , Extreme · 90% . What to keep is the Mode 's job, so picking one leaves Keep UVs and the Preserve options alone (before 2.7.0 they switched Keep UVs off). A .blend saved with one of the older built-in presets (from before 2.4.0) opens with the dropdown on Custom . Its values are kept. A preset you save stores: Reduction, Keep Normals, Keep UVs, the four Preserve options, and Sharp Angle, and applies all of them (the Mode then shows Custom ). It does not store the target count, Protect, Bake, Clean Mesh, or LOD settings. + — save the current values as a new preset. You type a name. Saving under the name of one of your own presets replaces it. You cannot use a built-in preset name. − — delete the selected preset. It is only enabled for presets you saved, and it asks you to confirm. Built-in presets cannot be deleted. Your presets are kept in the add-on preferences, so they stay after you restart Blender. Custom means no preset is selected. If you change Reduction, Keep Normals, Keep UVs, a Preserve option or Sharp Angle by hand, the dropdown goes back to Custom .
docs.title: Presets

docs.text: Under Keep Original in the Output group. It shows the most recent crush of the active crushed object: Object — the crushed object's name. Triangles — before → after. Total time — the whole crush for this object. Passes — how many passes the engine made. Click Details to see the time of each phase: Phase What it measures Extract Reading the source mesh Write Writing the input for the native binary Crush The native simplifier Read Reading the binary's output Build Creating the new Blender mesh and object Bake Normals Transferring the original's normals (Keep Normals) "Bake Normals" here is the Keep Normals transfer. It is not the normal map bake. When several objects are selected, their crushes run at the same time, so the phase timings can add up to more than the wall-clock time. That is expected. The numbers are only kept for the current Blender session. If you select an object that was not crushed in this session, it says there are no stats for it.

docs.text: Troubleshooting "Native binary not found" The addon ships with platform-specific simplifier binaries in its bin/ folder ( simplify-win-x86_64.exe , simplify-darwin-arm64 , simplify-linux-x86_64 , simplify-linux-arm64 ). The operator refuses to run if it can't find a binary matching your platform. If you see this: Re-install the addon from the official .zip — do not copy files manually Check that the binary exists at: <Blender extensions folder>/polygon_crusher_9000/bin/simplify-<your-platform> On macOS / Linux, the executable bit is restored automatically at runtime, but if your installer stripped it entirely, re-installing usually fixes it. Intel Macs have no bundled binary. There is no Python fallback. The result has more triangles than my target This is the most common question. Read the report in Blender's status bar. It shows the actual triangle count and usually says why. See Limits for the full list. The usual causes: "preserve options kept N tris" — only from versions before 2.7.1, where Borders, Materials, UV Seams and Sharp Edges were a hard lock. Since 2.7.1 a kept edge is a cost instead and the crush reaches the target. If you still see this on an old version, turn off the options you do not need, raise Sharp Angle , or raise the target. "the mesh may be broken: try Clean Mesh" — duplicate or zero-area faces blocked the crush. Turn on Clean Mesh and crush again. "it can't be reduced further without breaking the shape" — Clean Mesh was already on. The mesh is at its limit for this shape. Protect Area with a high Strength on a large area can leave the result above the target. Lower the Strength. A hole came out as a pentagon, or a crease flattened The target was too low for the number of edges you asked to keep. Since 2.7.1 the crush reaches the count you asked for even in Hard Surface mode, so at a very low count some kept lines have to give way. It picks the ones that change the shape least. Raise the target, turn off the Preserve options you do not need, or put a Protect Area on the part that must stay. See Hard Surface Preservation . Small parts disappeared At a heavy reduction the budget runs out and whole pieces go. Since 2.7.1 every separate piece keeps a minimum number of triangles until nothing else is left to remove, and then the smallest pieces go first; before, pieces went in whatever order they happened to collapse. Raise the target, or protect the pieces that must stay. If pieces are missing right after Clean Mesh , lower Remove Small Pieces : it deletes loose bits on purpose. See Limits . Sharp Edges kept almost nothing on my scan On a scan-like mesh, angle-based Sharp detection is skipped, because surface noise would make almost every edge sharp. Only edges you marked Sharp are kept. The report names the objects. Mark the edges you want to keep as Sharp in Blender, then crush again. See Limits . The report warns about non-manifold edges Very low targets on dense CAD meshes can fold hole walls together, leaving edges shared by three or more faces. Raise the target. See Limits . Crushed mesh looks faceted Keep Normals was probably off. Turn it on and crush again. If you baked a Normal Map , Keep Normals is greyed out on purpose. The crushed mesh uses its own smooth shading and the normal map carries the detail. Make sure the normal map is connected in the crushed mesh's material and the viewport is in Material Preview or Rendered mode. My baked maps do not show Workbench cannot show textures or normal maps. Crush switches a Workbench scene to EEVEE for you and tells you in the report. If you changed it back, switch the viewport to Material Preview. Base Color comes from the image textures feeding Base Color in the original's materials, or from vertex colors. If the report says an object has "no image texture or vertex colors", no base color was baked for it. A texture reported as "not loaded" is missing on disk: fix its path on the original and crush again. See Bake Maps and Auto UVs . Look in the folder you chose under Save To . For an unsaved .blend, the maps are packed into the file instead of saved as PNG files. Crusher ignored my modifiers It shouldn't — Polygon Crusher always reads the evaluated (post-modifier) mesh. If the result still looks like the un-modified base mesh, check that the modifier is actually visible in the viewport (the camera/eye toggles in the modifier properties panel). Anything hidden in the viewport is hidden from Polygon Crusher too. Blender freezes during crush Polygon Crusher runs the heavy work on a worker thread, so Blender should stay responsive. If the UI freezes: Very large meshes can take real time. Give it a few seconds. The progress bar on the Crush button updates as each object completes — if it's still moving, the run is healthy. Press ESC at any time to cancel. Where did my crushed object go? All crushed outputs are linked into a Crushed collection at the scene root (created automatically on the first crush). LOD chains go into a <name>_LODs collection inside it. The original object is either hidden (default) or deleted, depending on Keep Original . The Revert button is greyed out Revert needs a selected crushed object whose original still exists. It is greyed out when: the crushed object is not selected (the hidden original is not enough), the crush was made with Keep Original off, or you deleted the original. It is also greyed out while a crush is running. See Keep Original and Revert . Last Crush says "(No run yet)" Last Crush (in Advanced) only shows results for the active crushed object, from the current Blender session. If you select the original (or anything else), it says "No stats for" that object. Click a crushed object in the Crushed collection to see its timings. Contact Support Still having trouble? Email henriquevlopes@gmail.com

docs.text: Bake Maps and Auto UVs Crush can bake the original's detail onto the low-poly copy as texture maps. It connects the maps in the copy's materials, so the result looks right straight away. The Bake group in Advanced has two toggle buttons ( Sculpt mode opens it): Normal Map — bakes the original's surface detail. Base Color — bakes the original's color: its image textures, or its vertex colors. You can turn on one or both. Then click Crush as usual. After the crush, the progress bar shows "Baking" while the maps are made. Normal Map Bakes the original's surface detail into a normal map on the crushed mesh's UVs. The crushed mesh uses its own smooth shading instead of the Keep Normals transfer. This is what game engines expect. Keep Normals is greyed out while Normal Map is on. Normal Y picks the green channel convention. OpenGL (default) is for Blender, Unity and Godot. DirectX is for Unreal. A DirectX map still looks correct in Blender. The normal map is saved as Non-Color data. Base Color Bakes the original's color into a base color map on the crushed mesh's UVs, so a textured scan crushed to a fraction of its triangles still looks like the scan. Image textures first. For each material, the image feeding Base Color (directly, or through color nodes such as Mix or Hue/Saturation) is sampled through the original's own UVs. Materials with several textures are handled one by one, so a multi-material object gets one map with all of them in place. Vertex colors otherwise. A material with no image uses the object's active color attribute instead. Scans and ZBrush polypaint keep their color this way. Objects with neither are skipped, and the report says "no image texture or vertex colors". A texture whose file is missing is reported as "not loaded" and skipped. Auto UVs Baking needs UVs on the crushed mesh. Most scans and AI models have none, so Crush makes them. When: the original has no UVs, or Keep UVs is off. How: the mesh is split into a few large, projection-based islands. Each island is flattened, given equal texel density, and packed with a margin that fits the map size. Ask first: when an original has no UVs, Crush shows a dialog first: "No UVs to bake onto" with a Auto UV and Crush button. The dialog lists the objects that have no UVs. If Keep UVs is off, the crushed copy is unwrapped without a dialog. The report lists how many UV charts were made for each object. When baking, the borders of the UV islands are marked as seams and Sharp on the crushed mesh. This splits the smooth shading along the seams, so the normal map bakes without visible seams. If the original already has UVs and Keep UVs is on, those UVs are used for the bake. Overlapping UVs A bake writes each pixel of the map once. If two faces share the same UV space (stacked or mirrored islands, common in game assets), they fight over those pixels and the map is wrong there. With Keep UVs on, Crush checks for this and the report says so: it names the objects and how much of their map overlaps, and suggests turning Keep UVs off so the crushed copy is baked onto new UVs. Where the maps go Save To has two choices: Blend File Folder (default) — maps are saved as PNG files in the same folder as the .blend file. If the file is unsaved, the maps are packed into the .blend instead. The panel shows "Unsaved: maps get packed". Custom Folder — maps are saved as PNG files in the folder you pick. A path that starts with // is relative to the .blend file. Files are named <object name>_normal.png and <object name>_basecolor.png . Size sets the map resolution: 512, 1K, 2K (default) or 4K. How the maps are connected Each crushed mesh gets its own copies of its materials, named <object name>_<material name> . Your original materials are not changed. If the mesh has no material, Crush makes one. The normal map goes through a Normal Map node into the Principled BSDF Normal input. The base color map goes into Base Color . If an input was already connected in the copy, the old link is replaced. The report says how many inputs were replaced. Viewport Workbench cannot show textures or normal maps. If the render engine is Workbench, Crush switches the scene to EEVEE and puts Solid-mode 3D views into Material Preview. The report says when it did this. See also Limits for what baking cannot do.

docs.text: Rigs, Shape Keys and Vertex Colors The crushed copy keeps what the original carried per vertex. You don't need to re-rig, re-paint or re-bake anything. This happens on every crush, LOD and Budget part, with no setting to turn on. What carries over Vertex groups (skin weights). Every group of the original, with its weights. Armature modifier and parent. The crushed copy gets the same Armature modifier (same rig, same options) and the same parent as the original, so it poses, animates and moves with the rig. Shape keys. Every key with its value, slider range, relative key and vertex group mask. Vertex colors. The active color attribute: scan colors, ZBrush polypaint, AI-model colors. Each new vertex takes its values from the nearest point on the original's surface, so weights, shapes and colors stay smooth across the crushed mesh. docs.text: Clean Mesh AI-generated and scanned meshes often have broken geometry. When you crush them, they fall apart into fragments or stop far above the target. Clean Mesh repairs the mesh before the crush. Turn it on with the Clean Mesh checkbox in the Clean Mesh group of Advanced . Scan mode turns it on for you, and Auto turns it on when it finds something to repair. What it does Merges duplicate vertices. Removes broken faces (zero-area faces) and duplicate faces. Fixes flipped faces. Deletes small floating pieces (floaters). Remove Small Pieces The Remove Small Pieces slider (labelled Small Pieces in the panel) sets how small a loose piece has to be to get deleted. It is a share of the mesh's triangles. Default: 0.1% . Range: 0% to 5%. 0% keeps every piece. Greyed out unless Clean Mesh is on. Raise it when a scan has lots of floating bits. Keep it low for models that really are made of separate parts, like a set of small screws. Runs on its own when a mesh needs it You don't always have to switch it on. Clean Mesh runs by itself on an object (and the report says so) when: 2% or more of its vertices are duplicates. Scans from glTF, FBX and OBJ are often split along UV seams; crushing them without welding opens cracks along the seams. 2% or more of its triangles have no area. This is typical of an OBJ saved with too few decimals, or a scan snapped to a coarse grid. Without cleaning, the crush would stop with "Unable to reduce mesh". Welded meshes (most CAD parts and sculpts) score 0% and are left alone. Turn the checkbox on yourself for other broken meshes, for example flipped faces or floating debris. Scan Repair Scans bring their own kind of damage that welding does not touch. Under Clean Mesh there are three switches for it. They need Clean Mesh on, work with a crush from the panel and with Import and Crush , and the report says what they did. Cut Floor The table, turntable or ground captured under the model is removed. With Height at 0% the floor is found by itself: it is the dense, flat layer at the very bottom of the model. If the scan has no such layer, nothing is cut and the report says no floor found . Set Height to cut at a share of the model's height instead (everything below that goes). A ground scan (a patch of terrain) has a dense flat top of its own. That is not mistaken for a floor: only the lowest dense layer counts. Remove Spikes Two fixes in one switch: A point shot far out of the surface (farther than twice the size of its neighbour ring) is pulled back to the centre of that ring. A long stretched face, with an edge more than ten times the typical edge of the mesh, is deleted. Scanners make these where two surfaces got bridged. The small hole left behind is closed by Fill Holes. Fill Holes Small missing patches are closed with a fan of faces around a new centre point. Size is the longest outline a hole may have to be filled, as a share of the model's size (default 5%). Bigger openings stay open: the bottom of a bust, the back of a relief, the edge of a ground scan. The report counts the holes filled and the openings left open. Order Floor, spikes and stretched faces are handled first, then small floating pieces are removed, then holes are filled, then the winding is fixed so the new faces point the right way. The crush runs on the repaired mesh. Only the copy changes Clean Mesh only changes the crushed copy. Your original is never repaired or edited. When something was fixed, the report in the status bar lists it, for example how many vertices were merged and how many bad faces were removed. When to use it A crush ends far above the target and the report says the mesh may be broken: try Clean Mesh . The crushed result has holes, spikes or fragments that the original does not. The mesh comes from an AI model generator or a photogrammetry scan. If you already have Clean Mesh on and the report still says the mesh stays above the target, the mesh cannot be reduced further without breaking its shape. See Limits .

docs.text: Hard Surface Preservation Organic meshes (scans, sculpts) can be crushed freely. Hard-surface and CAD parts cannot. Holes must stay round, panel lines must stay straight, and material borders must stay where they are. The Preserve options keep those lines in place while everything else gets crushed. They are all off by default. The options Option What it keeps in place Borders Open borders: holes and cut edges. They do not shrink or wobble. Materials The borders between materials. UV Seams UV seam lines, so textures do not smear across them. Needs Keep UVs . Sharp Edges Edges you marked Sharp, plus any edge sharper than Sharp Angle . The crushed mesh also gets those sharp edges marked Sharp. One-click setup Hard Surface in the Mode menu turns on all four options and sets Sharp Angle to 30°. Auto picks it by itself on a mesh with flat faces and sharp edges. See Modes . You can also switch options on one at a time. For example, turn on only Materials to keep material borders on an organic mesh. How kept edges behave (2.7.1) Up to 2.7.0 a kept edge was a hard lock: the crush was not allowed to touch it at all. That had two costs. On a model with many borders, seams and creases (an electricity pole made of 103 parts) the crush ran out of edges it was allowed to collapse and stopped at about half the triangles, no matter what you asked for. And on a CAD block, the locked rims of the holes pushed every collapse into the faces next to them, so round holes came out as pentagons. Since 2.7.1 a kept edge is a cost instead of a lock . The crush spends its budget everywhere else first, and when it has to touch a kept line it collapses along the crease rather than across it, so the line stays a line. In practice: Hard Surface always reaches the count you asked for. The pole crushes to 2% with its structure intact; on the CAD block at keep 10% the holes stay round and the surface error is half of what it was. Small parts no longer vanish at heavy reductions. Every connected piece keeps a minimum number of triangles until the error budget is truly spent. Before, at keep 2% whole beams of the pole disappeared while small insulators floated on; now pieces go in order of how little they matter, smallest first, and only once nothing else is left to remove. Models with UVs no longer stop short of the target. With Low Distortion on (Hard Surface and Scan modes use it), the crush used to give up at around 12% above the target because it refused every collapse that touched a seam or might fold a UV face. It now tries the plain collapses first and only relaxes the UV rules, in stages, once the model is truly out of safe ones. Scans, sculpts and smooth CAD parts crush the same as before (within measurement noise). See the Benchmark for the numbers. Sharp Edges and Sharp Angle Sharp Edges uses two sources: Edges you marked Sharp in Blender. Edges where the two faces meet at more than Sharp Angle (default 30°). Bumps from scan noise do not count as sharp. An edge over the angle only counts when it sits next to flat faces or bends one way, like a real crease. On a mesh that reads as a scan (mostly noise, few flat faces), the angle test is skipped. Only the edges you marked Sharp are kept. The report names the objects where this happened. See Limits . UV Seams UV Seams needs Keep UVs to be on. If Keep UVs is off, the UV Seams button is greyed out. What a very low target costs Reaching the count is not free. Every kept edge is a line the crush would rather not touch, and the more of them there are, the sooner a low target forces it to. On a low-poly part with many creases, a target of a few hundred triangles means some of those lines give way: a hole loses a few sides, a chamfer flattens. The crush picks the lines that change the shape least, but check the result. If a line you care about gave way: Raise the target. Turn off the Preserve options you do not need, so the budget goes to the lines that matter. Raise Sharp Angle , so fewer edges count as sharp. Put a Protect Area on the part that must stay. See Limits for the full list. Presets Presets remember the four Preserve options and Sharp Angle . Save one preset for hard-surface work and one for organic meshes.

docs.text: Import and Crush Some scans are too big to open. A 500 MB OBJ from a photogrammetry app, a PLY with ten million faces: Blender's importer takes minutes, uses many gigabytes of memory, or fails. Import and Crush skips that step. The engine reads the file itself, crushes it, and only the crushed result is built in Blender. Find it as the Import and Crush... button under Crush in the panel, or in File > Import > Polygon Crusher: Import and Crush . How to use it Click Import and Crush... and pick an .obj , .ply or .stl file. In the file browser's side panel, set the target (same as in the panel), the Mode , Keep UVs (and textures) with Low Distortion , Clean Mesh with its Scan Repair switches and, for OBJ files, whether the file is Y up. In Auto the switches are greyed out: the engine sets them from what it finds in the file. Click Import and Crush . The progress bar under the panel shows "Reading" while the file loads and the crush percentage after that. The result appears in the Crushed collection, named after the file, shaded smooth and selected. The report in the status bar says how many triangles the file had, how many the result has, and how long it took. A 530 MB OBJ with 8.8 million triangles reads in about a second and crushes to 100,000 triangles in about eight seconds on a desktop PC. What comes along In the file On the result OBJ vt texture coordinates, PLY per-vertex or per-face texture coordinates The UV map (with Keep UVs on) OBJ materials ( usemtl ) and the .mtl file One material per name, faces assigned as in the file map_Kd in the .mtl , or a PLY TextureFile comment The texture, connected to Base Color, when the image is next to the file and Keep UVs is on Kd colour in the .mtl The material's Base Color, when there is no texture PLY vertex colours, OBJ v x y z r g b colours A Col vertex colour layer, connected to Base Color Quads and n-gons Triangulated Normals in the file are not used: the result is shaded smooth. Faces with more than four corners are split as fans, so a concave n-gon can come out wrong. Scans do not have those. Settings that apply The file browser has the same Mode menu as the panel. In Auto the engine looks at the file before it crushes it (which adds about the read time), and the report says which mode it picked and what it found. See Modes . From the panel: the Target , Keep UVs with Low Distortion , Clean Mesh with Remove Small Pieces and the three Scan Repair switches, and the four Hard Surface options (Borders, Materials, UV Seams and Sharp Edges with its angle). Keep Normals , Protect Area , Bake and LODs do not apply, because there is no original mesh in Blender to read them from. Crush the result again from the panel if you need a bake or LODs. Clean Mesh runs by itself when needed Most exported scans are split along their UV seams (every seam vertex is stored twice). Crushed as they are, they crack open along the seams. The engine checks the file and, when 2% or more of the vertices sit on another vertex, or 2% or more of the faces have no area, it runs Clean Mesh first. The report says so: "Clean Mesh ran by itself (file is split along its seams)". Textures The texture file has to be next to the model, as the .mtl or .ply names it. The add-on also looks for the file by its base name, ignoring case. When it is not found, the material is made without it and the report lists the missing names. With Keep UVs off there are no UVs to show a texture on, so the report asks you to turn it on. Tip An OBJ from most scanning apps and from Blender's own exporter is Y up. Leave OBJ is Y up on, and the model lands the way Blender's own importer would place it. For an OBJ that was written Z up, turn it off.

docs.text: LODs Tick Make LODs and Crush builds a full LOD chain in one click. How to use it Select the object. In the LODs group of Advanced , tick Make LODs . Set Levels (1 to 8, default 3). Set Ratio (5% to 95%, default 50%). Click Crush LODs . The main button changes its name while Make LODs is on. Each level keeps Ratio of the previous level's triangles. With the default 50% ratio and three levels, the chain is: Level Triangles kept LOD0 100% (the original) LOD1 50% LOD2 25% LOD3 12.5% When an object is active, the panel lists the exact triangle count of each level under the Levels and Ratio controls. A level never has fewer than 4 triangles. What you get Objects named <name>_LOD1 , <name>_LOD2 and so on. They go in a collection named <name>_LODs , inside the Crushed collection. The original stays as LOD0 . It is not hidden and not deleted. Every level is crushed from the original , not from the level before it. This gives each level the best surface for its triangle count. What changes while Make LODs is on The Target section (Percent, Count, Budget) is greyed out. LODs use their own Ratio. Keep Original is greyed out. LODs always keep the original. The triangle readout is hidden. Use the LOD list instead. Budget mode is not used. Each object gets its own chain. The Preserve, Protect Area and Clean Mesh settings still apply to every level. Revert Revert works on LODs. Select an LOD object and click Revert to delete it. See Keep Original and Revert . Limits The lowest levels of a hard-surface chain are where kept edges give way and small pieces go. Check them. See Limits .

docs.text: Modes Which switches suit a model is not obvious: a scan wants Clean Mesh and the scan repairs, a CAD part wants its edges kept in place, a sculpt wants neither. The Mode menu at the top of the panel picks them for you. Auto Auto is the default. When a mesh is selected, Auto asks the engine for a one-second look at it and shows what it sees under the menu, in plain words: Looks like a scan: rough surface all over Found: 120 spikes, 11 small holes It then applies the matching mode (Scan, Sculpt or Hard Surface) and, for a scan, switches on only the repairs it actually found: Cut Floor when there is a table or ground layer under the model, Remove Spikes when there are spikes or stretched faces, Fill Holes when there are small holes. Clean Mesh comes on when the mesh is split along its seams or full of collapsed faces, in any mode. How the engine decides: Hard surface : many flat faces meeting at sharp edges, or the long thin triangles of a CAD export. Scan : a rough surface everywhere (the faces around a typical point tilt by 8° or more) and almost no flat patches. Sculpt : everything else, which is to say a smooth surface. Auto looks again whenever the selected mesh's triangle count changes, and only in Object Mode. With several meshes selected it looks at the active one and applies the result to the whole crush. Meshes over 600,000 triangles do not get looked at by themselves (it would take a few seconds on every selection). A Detect button appears instead; a crush in Auto mode always looks first anyway. Auto's guess can be wrong on a mesh between two kinds (a smoothed hard-surface model, a very clean scan). Pick the mode yourself in that case. Scan For 3D scans and photogrammetry. Clean Mesh on, with Remove Spikes and Fill Holes (and Cut Floor when a table was found), Keep Normals, Keep UVs with Low Distortion when the mesh has UVs. Nothing is kept in place: scan noise has no edges worth keeping. The Clean Mesh and Preserve groups open in Advanced. Sculpt For sculpts and smooth organic models. Keep Normals and Keep UVs (when there are UVs), nothing else forced. The Protect Area and Bake groups open, because a face to protect and a normal map to keep the detail are what a sculpt usually needs. Hard Surface For CAD and mechanical models. Borders , Materials , UV Seams (when there are UVs) and Sharp Edges at 30° are kept in place, with Keep Normals and Keep UVs (when there are UVs). Since 2.7.1 the kept edges are a cost rather than a lock, so this mode reaches the count you asked for. See Hard Surface Preservation . The Preserve group opens. Custom Your own settings; every Advanced group opens. Changing any value a mode controls (Keep Normals, Keep UVs, Low Distortion, the four Preserve options, Sharp Angle, Clean Mesh and the Scan Repair switches) turns the menu into Custom (from Scan) , and a Reset to Scan defaults button under it brings the mode's values back. Protect Area, Bake, LODs, the amount and Keep Original are never touched by a mode. Import and Crush The file browser has the same Mode menu. In Auto , the engine looks at the file before it crushes it, which adds about the time it takes to read the file (a second or so for a 500 MB OBJ); the report says which mode it picked and what it found. See Import and Crush .

docs.text: Protect Areas Some parts of a mesh matter more than the rest: a face, hands, text on a label. Protect Area keeps their detail while the rest gets crushed. It is its own group inside Advanced ; Sculpt mode opens it. How to use it Select the object and press Tab for Edit Mode. Select the faces, edges or vertices you want to keep. Under Protect Area , click Add . The selection goes into a vertex group named Protected , and the field under the buttons shows it. Set Strength and Blur if the defaults don't suit you. Turn on Show Heatmap to check the result in the viewport. Click Crush . To take parts back out, select them in Edit Mode and click Remove . Add and Remove only work in Edit Mode. Until an area is set, the panel shows a hint: "Edit Mode: select faces, then Add". Using your own vertex group You can also paint a vertex group yourself (Weight Paint mode, or assign weights in Edit Mode) and pick it in the field. When the active object is a mesh, the field lists its vertex groups. Higher weights keep more detail. With a group picked, Add puts the selection into that group. Strength Strength Effect 0% No protection 50% (default) Protected areas keep noticeably more detail 100% Protected areas are nearly frozen The slider is not linear. The protection grows faster as you move towards 100%. Blur Protection fades out softly from the marked area instead of stopping at a hard line. Blur sets how far, as a share of the object's size. The default is 5% . 0% makes a hard edge. Show Heatmap Colors the selected objects in the viewport by how strongly each part is protected, with the Blur fade included: blue is free to crush, red is fully protected. It updates as you add, remove or change Blur, including in Edit Mode. It is only a viewport overlay; nothing is added to your scene. Strength and Blur are greyed out until a Protect Area is set. Good to know The group is read after modifiers, so it matches the mesh you see in the viewport. The group name is matched on every selected object. Objects that do not have a group with that name are crushed normally. If the group exists but has no weights, the object is crushed without protection and Blender shows a warning. Protect Area works with all three target modes . Strong protection on large areas can leave the result above the target triangle count. Check the after count in the report. See Limits .
